headline: Cleaner New York air linked to higher toddler scores

sources.title: Clean Air Policies Linked to Improved Cognition Among New York City Children (Columbia Mailman School of Public Health)
Less air pollution previously related to clean air and climate policies is linked to improved cognitive scores over time in NYC children (Environmental Health)
Clean Air Policies Help Kids Breathe and Think Better (Inside Climate News)
Cleaner city air linked to better cognitive development in children (Earth.com)

chunks.text: New York City children scored higher on tests of early [[mental development]] as the air their mothers breathed during [[pregnancy]] got cleaner, Columbia University reports. The study {{came out}} in the [[journal]] Environmental Health on August 15, 2026. The team followed more than 1,000 mother-child pairs who {{signed up}} between 1998 and 2020 in Northern Manhattan and the South Bronx, two [[low-income]] areas where the children {{grew up}}.

chunks.text: Columbia says [[fine particles]] {{went down}} 32 percent and nitrogen dioxide 30 percent from 1998 to 2016. A group of [[harmful chemicals]] from burning [[fossil fuels]] fell 60 percent from 1998 to 2020. Pregnant women wore backpack [[monitors]] to measure those chemicals, and the other [[pollutants]] were [[estimated]] at each home. The children were tested at ages 1, 2, and 3. Scores at age 3 {{went up}} 26 percent between the earliest and latest groups, after the team {{factored in}} the mother's education, the child's sex, and smoking in the home.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher level

chunks.text: The researchers link the cleaner air to policies the city {{brought in}} during those years. The Clean Fuel Bus Program and Clean Air Taxi [[legislation]] {{cut down on}} [[traffic emissions]]. The Clean Heat Program {{phased out}} dirty [[heating oil]] in buildings, and the Climate Mobilization Act required larger buildings to reduce [[greenhouse gases]]. "Policies to reduce fossil fuel emissions benefit developing brains," said the Columbia professor who led the study, adding that the results support efforts to {{keep up}} the cuts.

verbs.wrong: To mention a subject for discussion
verbs.why: The school brought in a ban on cell phones, and the state brought in a new speed limit last year. New York City brought in several clean-air policies during the years of the study.

verbs.correct: To end the use of something gradually
verbs.why: The airline phased out its oldest planes, and many stores have phased out plastic bags. The Clean Heat Program phased out dirty heating oil in New York buildings.

verbs.correct: To continue at the same level
verbs.why: It is hard to keep up a diet on vacation, and the team kept up its winning streak all season. The Columbia professor who led the study said the results support efforts to keep up the cuts in emissions.

chunks.text: The team {{set out}} to test whether cleaner air from these policies was linked to better [[cognitive scores]], the first study to do so over 20 years. It has limits. Only 1,109 of the 1,446 children had test results, so the rest were {{left out}}. The authors also {{point out}} that changes the study did not measure, such as [[shifts]] in the neighborhoods, could {{account for}} part of the [[gains]].

mainIdea.s: Researchers followed New York City families for over 20 years as pollution from traffic and heating fell. Cleaner air during pregnancy was linked to higher early development scores in children.
mainIdea.why: More than 1,000 mother-child pairs were followed from 1998 to 2020, and scores at age 3 went up 26 percent as fine particles, nitrogen dioxide, and the chemicals from fossil fuels fell.

mainIdea.s: A 20-year study found that New York City children scored higher on development tests as air pollution fell. The researchers say the cleaner air came mainly from the closing of old factories.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the researchers link the cleaner air to city policies on buses, taxis, heating oil, and building emissions, not to factory closings.

mainIdea.s: New York City has passed a law requiring every school bus to run on electricity by 2035. Health officials say the change will protect children from harmful exhaust in their daily commute.
mainIdea.why: There was no new school bus law. The study looked at policies passed between 1998 and 2020 and at how children's test scores changed as the air got cleaner.

lines.text: Did you see the Columbia study that {{came out}} last month? The one about air pollution and kids in New York.
I saw the headline. Cleaner air, better test scores?
Pretty much. They followed more than a thousand mothers and children who {{signed up}} between 1998 and 2020, all in Northern Manhattan and the South Bronx.
That's a long time. What did they measure?
Three pollutants during pregnancy. Fine particles {{went down}} 32 percent, nitrogen dioxide 30 percent, and a group of harmful chemicals from burning fossil fuels 60 percent.
[[Those are real numbers]]. And the kids?
Tested at ages 1, 2, and 3. Scores at age 3 {{went up}} 26 percent from the earliest group to the latest, even after they {{factored in}} things like the mother's education.
[[Good news for once]]. So what cleaned the air?
City policies, they say. Cleaner buses and taxis {{cut down on}} traffic emissions, and the Clean Heat Program {{phased out}} dirty heating oil in buildings.
[[Credit where it's due]], then. Those policies took more than twenty years to pass.
Right, and the lead researcher wants the city to {{keep up}} the cuts. She said cleaner air benefits developing brains.
[[Is there a catch?]] There's usually a catch.

A couple. Only 1,109 of the 1,446 children had test results, so the rest were {{left out}}. And the authors {{point out}} that other changes in the neighborhoods could {{account for}} some of the gains.
[[Points for saying so]]. It still seems like a strong result.
That's how I read it. [[Hard to argue with]] twenty years of data.
